feedback: If a learner stops at 'oxygen is delivered', prompt: what does the same blood carry on the way back? (carbon dioxide) — the loop is two-way, not one-way delivery.
If a learner says cells 'breathe air', clarify: cells receive oxygen FROM the blood, not from air directly; only the lungs take gases directly from the air.
If a learner treats the heart and lungs as unrelated, have them re-trace the oxygen from alveolus through blood and heart to the muscle so the handoff is explicit.
If a learner says oxygen is 'used up and that's the end', point to the CO2 produced that must be carried away and exhaled — the loop closes.
activities.intendedInsight: The circulatory and respiratory systems are coupled into one continuous loop with two exchange points; blood simultaneously carries oxygen body-ward and carbon dioxide lung-ward.
learnerActions: Trace ONE oxygen molecule across the complete circuit: alveolus → into the blood → to the heart → out through an artery → into a working muscle cell.
At the muscle cell, name what the cell does with the oxygen: uses it to release energy from food, producing carbon dioxide waste.
Now follow ONE carbon dioxide molecule the other way: from the muscle cell → into the blood → back to the lungs → breathed out.
State at each end what is being swapped: gas exchange at the alveolus (oxygen into the blood, CO2 out of the blood) and gas exchange at the body cell (oxygen out of the blood, CO2 into the blood).
Say in your own words why this is really ONE system, not two: blood is the shared carrier linking the lungs to every cell, carrying oxygen one way and carbon dioxide the other at the same time.
activities.title: Follow one molecule around the whole loop

feedback: If a learner says breathing speeds up 'to cool you down', clarify: your body cools down mainly by sweating; the main reason breathing speeds up is to bring in more oxygen and blow off more carbon dioxide.
If a learner says the rates rise 'because you're tired', reframe: the rise happens to MEET demand as muscles work hard, not because of tiredness.
If a learner says the heart beats faster 'so you don't faint', redirect to the oxygen-demand driver: muscles need more oxygen delivered and more waste removed.
If a learner treats the two rates as unrelated coincidences, link them: both serve the same demand, so both respond together.
activities.intendedInsight: Heart rate and breathing rate rise together during exercise because the same coupled system must deliver more oxygen (used to release energy from food) and clear more waste (carbon dioxide) to meet muscle demand.
learnerActions: Measure your resting pulse (beats per minute) and count your resting breaths per minute.
Do vigorous activity (e.g. star jumps) for one minute; notice your breathing speeding up as you go.
Immediately re-measure your pulse and breaths per minute and record the before/after pair.
Describe what your data show: did your pulse and your breathing rate both go up? (They usually both rise after vigorous exercise; if yours didn't, check how and when you measured.)

Reason from the data to the cause: working muscles suddenly needed MORE oxygen and produced MORE carbon dioxide, so breathing rose to exchange more gas at the lungs and the heart rose to pump that oxygen-rich blood round faster and carry the waste back.

Extension – preview the healthy-lifestyle link: a fitter body delivers oxygen more efficiently, so with practice a person's systems can meet the same demand more easily; this is a first step toward why fitness and exercise matter.
activities.title: Resting vs exercise: measure, then reason to WHY

feedback: Full understanding: explains muscles demand more oxygen and make more CO2; breathing rises to exchange gas and the heart rises to pump it round — one integrated system — and can reason about recovery or a broken link.
Partial understanding: knows muscles need more oxygen and both rates rise, but describes the systems as separate facts; re-run the single-molecule trace to connect lungs→blood→heart→muscle.
Gap: treats heart and lungs as unrelated or explains the faster rates by cooling or tiredness; return to the measurement activity and reason from the data to oxygen demand.

For the broken-link probe: harder breathing alone cannot get much extra oxygen to the legs if the heart does not speed up, because blood would still flow at about its resting rate; the heart must pump the oxygen-rich blood round faster to deliver more — this exposes whether the learner truly sees the coupling.
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing, prediction, and data interpretation consolidate the coupled model and check whether the learner can trace oxygen lungs→blood→heart→muscle as one linked delivery system.
learnerActions: Put the coupled cycle steps in order: oxygen into blood at lungs → heart pumps oxygenated blood to body → cells use oxygen and make CO2 → blood returns CO2 to lungs → breathed out.
Predict what happens to pulse and to breaths per minute when moving from rest to running, and state WHY both change.
Interpret a resting-vs-exercise data table and explain what the numbers show about the body's demand.
Answer the probe: where does the oxygen your legs need get INTO the blood, and what carries it from there to the legs?
Answer the recovery probe: after you stop running, why do your heart and breathing stay fast for a while before settling?
Answer the broken-link probe: if your lungs worked harder but your heart did NOT speed up, would much extra oxygen reach your legs? Explain your answer.
activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, predict, and interpret data
